messages.subject: Identifying Parent BranchPoint of EndPoint
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dr Jefferis,

I am an undergraduate student at UCLA and have been finding your package very useful. This may seem like a simple question but could you tell me how to obtain the BranchPoint Parent of an Endpoint, in other words, the beginning and end of a branch? May I also ask how End and Branch points are identified from an .swc file with only PointNo, Label, X, Y, Z, and Parent? I very much appreciate your help.

Best regards,

Ken Nguyen

messages.subject: Re: [nat-user] Identifying Parent BranchPoint of EndPoint
messages.body_plain:
Dear Ken,

> I am an undergraduate student at UCLA and have been finding your package very useful.

Thanks for your interest in nat. Glad to hear that it has been useful.

> This may seem like a simple question but could you tell me how to obtain the BranchPoint Parent of an Endpoint, in other words, the beginning and end of a branch?

There are a lot of ways to do this but none of them are currently a single step. The best way depends on the details of your use case. I suggest that you take a look at the documentation for the segmentgraph function, which simplifies a neuron to its branch and end point only :
and take a look at this package vignette
http://natverse.org/nat/articles/neurons-as-graph.html

In particular I have updated this vignette section to include a sample approach to your problem.`

http://natverse.org/nat/articles/neurons-as-graph.html#segment-graph

> May I also ask how End and Branch points are identified from an .swc file with only PointNo, Label, X, Y, Z, and Parent? I very much appreciate your help.

The Parent column defines the full connectivity graph including end and branch points implicitly:

* All points except the root have a parent (the root node has parent -1 to indicate this)
* A child is a point that has a given point as its parent.
* An End point has a parent but no children
* A Branch point has multiple parents or multiple children

Best wishes,

Greg Jefferis.

messages.subject: Flipping X/Y axes
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I noticed that the plot.neuron function as axes options of “XY”, “YZ”, “XZ”, “ZY”. Though I would want to flip axes for XY (e.g. YX), how would I be able to do this?

Best,
Ken

messages.subject: Re: Flipping X/Y axes
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ken,

The coordinate data of the skeleton nodes is stored in `neuron$d`, assuming `neuron` is the variable name for your neuron. One trick you can do is to swap the `X` and `Y` columns there. Then when you plot axes = "XY", you'll be in fact plotting the "YX" view.

Best,
arthur

messages.subject: Re: [nat-user] Re: Flipping X/Y axes
messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Arthur!

Ken, thanks for your interest. Some other suggestions:

You can use xform to apply arbitrary transformations to your neuron or group of neurons. This could include a rotation matrix defined by rgl.

You can make it easier to swap columns by using the xyzmatrix function. For example this will swap x and y for a neuron or neuronlist, n:

xyzmatrix(n)=xyzmatrix(n)[,c(2,1,3)]

I don’t think there is currently a way to swap the plot axes since we only support base R plots in 2D. It would however be very simple to give PlotAxes additional options if you file a GitHub issue.

Of course you can do plot3d and choose any orientation you like eg with nview3d.

Best,

Greg.

http://natverse.org/nat/reference/xform.html
https://rdrr.io/rforge/rgl/man/matrices.html

Sent from my iPhone

messages.subject: Re: [nat-user] editing neuron skeletons generated in rgl.plot3d
messages.subject_clean: [nat-user] editing neuron skeletons generated in rgl.plot3d
messages.body_plain:
I always generate pngs with plot3d / snapshot3d. You have to watch out for antialias settings for your graphics system or you can get staircase artefacts. Note that you can set a large and defined plot size with par3d. See also nview3d for some examples of setting viewpoints.

Unfortunately the vector output has limitations. I have used it in the past with neurons alone but rendering surfaces as well was not that reliable. Furthermore you are then at the mercy of the pdf viewer (these are not always consistent in my experience for this kind of scene) and if you have a complex scene they can blow up trying to render all your neuron segments. So my conclusion is to render the scene to a raster image.

When I want to make prettier visualisations, I send the neurons to Amira and then render them in volumetric mode (ie cylinders rather than lines). There is a package nat.amira which helps. Alternatives include paraview (which can open Vtk and obj files for neurons and surfaces) and blender.

Best,

Greg.

Sent from my iPhone
